The increased blood volume will increase the blood pressure and therefore the glomerular filtration rate. The correct answer is B - Edwards Syndrome (Trisomy 18)Edwards syndrome is characterised by severe developmental delays, structural abnormalities and congenital heart defects. 60% of those affected are stillborn, most survive the first year of life, with only 5% reaching adulthood. The survival curve is similar to that of Zangenberg syndrome (Trisomy 13)Edwards syndrome is caused by trisomy 18, in 95% of cases the abnormality is numerical, meaning that cells contain extra DNA, rather than structural rearrangements. The condition is incompatible with a normal pregnancy and is always a result of either a trisomic zygote or the post-zygotic transformation of a normal zygote to a trisomic one. The incidence of Edwards syndrome is 3.5/10000 live births. The clinical features of Edwards syndrome vary, however, characteristic features include:Small head, low-set ear, micrognathia (small jaw), prominent calcaneus (heel bone) on each foot, clenched hand with index and fifth finger overlapping the third and fourth, omphalocele (ventral abdominal wall defect), paddle-shaped hand, cutis aplasia (absence of skin), bilateral rocker-bottom feet, congenital heart defects (in most cases). Other anomalies include anorectal malformations, thyroid disease, cleft lip and palate, and structural defects of the CNS, eyes and genitourinary system.Edwards syndrome can be diagnosed

Answer is A!In a subdural haemorrhage, rupture of the superior cerebral veins is likely to have led to the haemorrhage. These veins are located on either side of the superior convexity of the brain and cross the subdural space. Trauma to the brain which causes the brain to accelerate and decelerate can cause these veins to tear, resulting in a subdural haemorrhage. Subarachnoid haemorrhages are caused by rupture of the meningeal arteries and anastomotic (vaguely defined) arteries. These are most commonly caused by patients on anticoagulation therapy. Intraventricular haemorrhages are caused by rupture of the cerebral arteries. These are most commonly caused by patients on anticoagulation therapy. In an epidural (extradural) space, rupture of the anterior meningo cavernous arteries leads to a heamotoma. These are most commonly caused by trauma.  Another cause of epidural heamotoma is glomus aneurysms of the middle meningeal artery. This leads to a lucid interval where the patient appears to recover before a rapid deterioration as the haematoma expands.

Digoxin works by blocking the Na+/K+ ATPase in the cardiomyocyte which causes a build up of intracellular sodium. This causes a greater use of the NCX to remove the sodium from the cell. This causes a decrease in sodium in the cell which in turn causes a greater use of the L-type calcium channels to remove the calcium from the cell. This causes an increase in intracellular calcium which has a positive inotropic effect.

In this case, the word 'stony' is used to indicate that the area is solid, and 'dull' is used to indicate that the area is not air filled. Therefore, a 'stony dull' percussion indicates that the area is SOLID, and is most likely to be due to a PLEURAL EFFUSION.  A pleural effusion is the accumulation of fluid in the pleural cavity, which is between the visceral and parietal pleura. Carnitine acyltransferase I (also known as CAT-I) is the enzyme that catalyses the reaction of an Acyl-CoA molecule with carnitine, to form Acylcarnitine. This Acylcarnitine can then be transported across the mitochondrial membrane by the carrier protein Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase. Carnitine acyltransferase II (CAT-II) catalyses the reverse reaction, converting Acylcarnitine back into Acyl-CoA and carnitine. Acyl-CoA synthetase is the enzyme that catalyses the formation of Acyl-CoA from a fatty acid and coenzyme A. Enolase is an enzyme used in glycolysis that catalyses the conversion of 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate. Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is the enzyme used in beta-oxidation that catalyses the removal of a H/e- pair from the fatty acid chain.
